sentences.text: Savannasaurus was a medium-sized titanosaur reaching approximately 15 meters in length, weighing around 20 tons, and standing about 3 meters high at the shoulder.
This animal possessed wide hips exceeding 1.1 meters at their widest points, a trait likely aiding navigation through muddy floodplains.

Researchers identified an undulating front articulating surface on one tail vertebra and noted vertebral traits that increased spinal flexibility, such as the absence of hyposphene-hypantrum articulations.
The first specimen was discovered in March 2005 by David Elliot and his family, leading to the naming of Savannasaurus elliottorum in 2016 by Stephen Poropat and colleagues.
Fossils were found in the Late Cretaceous Winton Formation of Queensland, Australia, where the holotype specimen, nicknamed "Wade," is held at the Australian Age of Dinosaurs museum.
The specimen was preserved within a siltstone concretion that required splitting with jackhammers and chisels to allow for reassembly.
Savannasaurus is classified within the unranked family Titanosauria and is considered an early-diverging member, though not part of the specialized group Lithostrotia.
Analyses suggest its ancestors migrated to Australia through Antarctica around 105 to 100 million years ago, with palaeobiogeographic data indicating they were likely Asian in origin.

Associated teeth suggest the theropod Australovenator may have fed on the holotype, while the unusual astragalus form was possibly an adaptation for weight-bearing, though this remains unclear due to missing hindlimb bones.

A 2017 analysis placed Savannasaurus and Diamantinasaurus successively basal to a clade containing Baotianmansaurus and Dongyanosaurus, while a 2019 study found it within Saltasauridae only when using equal weighting.
Savannasaurus lived during the Cenomanian to Lower Turonian stages of the Late Cretaceous, a time when the Australian region it inhabited was located at 70°S latitude with a cool, temperate climate.
Geographic models suggest its ancestors had ranges spanning South America, Africa, and Indo-Madagascar.
Researchers noted the possibility that hyposphene-hypantrum articulations, which typically argue against a basal position, could have evolved independently multiple times among titanosaurs.
